summary.heading: Describing oscillations
summary.html:
• An oscillation is a repeated back-and-forth motion about an equilibrium position (where the object would rest if left alone).
  • Displacement $x$: distance and direction from equilibrium (can be negative). Amplitude $x_0$: the maximum displacement, half the distance between the two extremes.
  • Time period $T$: time for one complete oscillation. Frequency $f$: oscillations per second (Hz). Angular frequency $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, which links SHM to circular motion.
$$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$$

summary.heading: The conditions for SHM
summary.html:
• SHM happens when the resultant force (and so the acceleration) is proportional to the displacement and always directed towards the equilibrium position: a restoring force.
$$a = -\omega^2 x$$
  • The minus sign shows the acceleration is always opposite to the displacement, which is what pulls the object back. An $a$–$x$ graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient $-\omega^2$.
  • Mass on a spring: $F = -kx$ and $F = ma$ give $a = -\frac{k}{m}x$, so $\omega^2 = \frac{k}{m}$.
  • The period doesn't depend on the amplitude (the motion is isochronous): a bigger oscillation has further to go but moves faster.

summary.heading: Graphs of SHM
summary.html:
• Displacement, velocity and acceleration all vary sinusoidally with the same period, each a quarter of a cycle out of step with the one before.
  • At the extremes ($x = \pm x_0$): velocity zero, acceleration maximum (towards equilibrium).
  • At equilibrium ($x = 0$): speed maximum, acceleration zero.
  • The $a$–$t$ graph is the $x$–$t$ graph upside down (the minus sign). Velocity = gradient of the $x$–$t$ graph; acceleration = gradient of the $v$–$t$ graph.

summary.heading: The mass–spring system and the simple pendulum
summary.html:
$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} \qquad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$$
  • Mass–spring: a larger mass gives a longer period, a stiffer spring a shorter one. It doesn't depend on $g$ or the amplitude, so it works the same on the Moon.
  • Pendulum: SHM only for small swings (below about 10°). The period depends on $l$ and $g$, not on the bob's mass or the (small) amplitude.
  • Proportionalities: $T \propto \sqrt{m}$ for a spring, $T \propto \sqrt{l}$ for a pendulum (four times the length doubles the period).
  • Measuring $g$: time 20 oscillations to reduce the effect of reaction time, repeat for several lengths and plot $T^2$ against $l$: a straight line through the origin with gradient $\frac{4\pi^2}{g}$.

summary.heading: Energy in SHM
summary.html:
• Energy is continually transferred between kinetic and potential energy (elastic for a spring, gravitational for a pendulum).
  • At the extremes: $E_k = 0$, potential energy maximum. At equilibrium: $E_k$ maximum, potential energy minimum.
  • With no damping, the total energy is constant.
  • $E_k$ and $E_p$ each peak twice per period, so they vary at twice the frequency of the oscillation.
  • At SL, describe these changes in words and sketches; HL students also calculate them.

summary.heading: Phase and the equations of SHM
summary.html:
• SHM is the shadow of uniform circular motion. The phase is the angle $\omega t + \phi$; the phase angle $\phi$ is its value at $t = 0$, in radians.
$$x = x_0\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ $$v = \omega x_0\cos(\omega t + \phi)$$ $$v = \pm\,\omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2}$$
  • $\phi = 0$: starts at equilibrium moving in the positive direction. $\phi = \frac{\pi}{2}$: starts at $+x_0$.
  • Maximum speed $v_{\max} = \omega x_0$, at $x = 0$.
  • A phase difference $\Delta\phi$ corresponds to a time difference $\Delta t = \frac{\Delta\phi}{2\pi}T$ (a quarter cycle is $\frac{\pi}{2}$, half a cycle is $\pi$).
  • Differentiating $x$ twice gives $a = -\omega^2 x$, confirming the equations describe SHM.
  • Calculator in radians.

summary.heading: Energy in SHM: calculations
summary.html:
$$E_T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2 \qquad E_p = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$ $$E_k = E_T - E_p = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2(x_0^2 - x^2)$$
  • Total energy $\propto$ amplitude squared: doubling $x_0$ gives four times the energy.
  • At half the amplitude, $E_p$ is only a quarter of the total, so three-quarters is kinetic.
  • For a spring, $m\omega^2 = k$, so $E_p = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ (as in A.3).

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Taking the amplitude as the distance between the extremes (that is $2x_0$).
  • Leaving out or not explaining the minus sign in $a = -\omega^2 x$.
  • Saying the velocity is greatest at the extremes: it is zero there, and the acceleration is greatest.
  • Thinking a heavier pendulum bob changes the period (it doesn't; for a mass–spring system the mass does).
  • Using $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for large swings.
  • HL A calculator in degrees with $\sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
  • HL Assuming $E_k = E_p$ at half the amplitude.

Models: List the assumptions behind the SHM model of a pendulum. Which one fails first as the swing gets bigger, and how would you notice?
A guitar note looks messy on an oscilloscope, yet it can be built from simple sine waves. Does that make SHM a description of reality or a tool for calculation?
Observations: Galileo timed swings against his pulse. How reliable is that as a clock, and what would he have needed to show the period really is independent of amplitude?
Ask students to test isochronism themselves with a pendulum and a stopwatch. At what amplitude can they first detect a change in period?
Measurement and a shared endeavour: Why does every country need to agree on one definition of the second? What would go wrong for GPS or the internet if they didn't?
Why is an atomic oscillation a better time standard than a pendulum or a quartz crystal?

oracy.activity: Explain it to a younger student
oracy.html:
Explain it to a younger student (pairs, 6 minutes, then swap roles): one explains; the other plays a curious 12-year-old who keeps asking "why?". Question: "Why does a pendulum take the same time for each swing whether you pull it back a little or a bit further?"

  • Think of it like this: …
  • That happens because …
  • So, putting it together, …

Listen for: a bigger displacement gives a bigger restoring force and acceleration, so the bob moves faster over the longer path; this holds only for small amplitudes.

When is a simple model good enough?: Give students the pendulum equation and a 30° swing. Is the error big enough to matter for a clock, for a playground swing, for an exam answer?
Who decides the threshold: the person building the model or the person using its results?
What counts as proof?: Fourier's methods worked before mathematicians could fully justify them. Should results that work be accepted before the reasoning is complete?
Compare proof in mathematics with evidence in physics. Which one does a physicist need before using a technique?
Is nature made of sine waves, or is that: A square wave can be built from sine waves, but sine waves can also be built from square waves. Does that weaken the claim that nature is made of sine waves?
Is a mathematical description something we discover or something we choose?
Can a definition be wrong?: If the second is defined by caesium, what does it mean when two caesium clocks disagree?
Ask students for other definitions that changed over time (the metre, the kilogram). Were the old definitions wrong, or just less useful?

videos.title: Pendulum Waves
videos.use: Fifteen pendulums of slightly different lengths drift in and out of step. A striking hook for $T \propto \sqrt{l}$: ask students why each pendulum has a different period.

videos.title: 1D10.50 Simple Harmonic Motion and Uniform Circular Motion
videos.use: The shadow of a rotating object matches an oscillating mass. Use it to introduce angular frequency and (HL) the phase angle.

videos.title: The Surprising Secret of Synchronization
videos.use: Extension: metronomes on a shared platform fall into step. Good for discussing oscillators that interact, and a link to resonance in C.4.
